newsitem.title: UK: Britain not liable for EU pensions says Euro group.
newsitem.headline: Britain not liable for EU pensions says Euro group.

text.p: Britain will not be liable to fund the pensions of other European countries if it joins the single currency and would probably benefit from it, a study published on Wednesday from the Action Centre for Europe (ACE) says.

Contrary to conclusions drawn by a British parliamentary Social Security Select Committee in a report in October last year, the UK "could stand to gain in a Monetary Union from its private pensions expertise and its relatively low liabilities".

"The (parliamentary) report has provided a misleading account...this (ACE report) has demonstrated that the existance of unfunded pensions liabilities in continental Europe is no reason for Britain not to join a single currency."
The report from the centre, whose president is former Conservative Party Chancellor Geoffrey Howe, did not dispute that most European nations face a pensions funding crisis.

It quoted the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development saying that by 2035 Italy will be spending some 21.5 percent of its gross domestic product on pensions, with Germany and France spending 18.5 percent and 14.5 percent respectively.
Britain's pension bills will be just over five percent of GDP, only a little more than its current expenditure.
But it was a fallacy, ACE said, that Britons would have to pay higher taxes to fund pensions elsewhere in Europe.

"Article 104b of the Maastricht Treaty (the No-Bail-Out Clause) explicitly rules out such a sharing of liabilities," the report said. "Unquestionably, dealing with pensions liabilities is strictly an issue for national governments, a fact that is reinforced by the European Union's principle of subsidiarity."

It said member states will have to fund pension liabilities by increasing national taxation or reducing spending in other areas and that discipline will be enforced by the Stability and Growth Pact championed by France and Germany, and market forces.
Members straying from the pact will be heavily fined by the European Council of Finance. The report said it would be in Britain's interests to make the Stability Pact successful.
Moves towards fiscal harmonisation in the EU, which has rung alarm bells in the UK, was indeed a long term goal for the single market, but Britain could always exercise its veto.
Furthermore, it was "arrogant" to assume that Britain was the only EU member which had thought about tackling pensions funding. Reform was well under way in Italy, Germany and France.

The report also challenged the parliamentary committee recommendation that pension liabilities be regarded as fixed public debt. "Pensions debts' do not accrue interest and are not legally binding obligations," it said. "They are merely government promises that can be broken."

"Britain has future debts' arising from the decommissioning of nuclear power stations and from obligations under the Public Finance Initiative. Theoretical pensions debts' should be regarded in the same way."
